name: Rafael Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. This is confidential, so please say what you'd tell others and what you think privately. What is your usual day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Rafael, 43, and I took a two-year college diploma after years in a warehouse. I'm still a junior developer at a tech company, checking the files that bring clinic appointments into our software; I like finding a wrong date before a patient makes the trip. I use an AI helper now and then on test data, but I need the senior developer to explain the tricky fixes, and I leave on time when my partner has a care night shift and our two children need dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people the little AI helper can draft a data check, but I still have to run it against real appointment records. I use it now and then when another developer has shown me a safe way to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job might stay about the same, but money already feels tight. I'm 43, a junior developer on a lower wage after a two-year diploma, and we have about three weeks of bills saved; my partner works night shifts in care, and we still have a mortgage and two children at school. There are not many software employers nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking appointment imports each morning and asking the senior developer to review the parts I cannot follow. If my partner's shifts and mine hold, we'd move 15 from each payday into a school-expense pot in the first year, and use the helper only on test records without names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household, not the small tool. A missed night shift is more frightening this month than a forecast about code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the helper nearly get wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When a clinic sends a date in the wrong format, patients can end up booked for the wrong day. Last week the helper suggested a neat fix that would have moved every afternoon slot, so I asked the senior developer before touching the real records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the school-expense pot for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school pot is for shoes and bus fares, not a holiday. If one of us loses shifts, the 15 stays in the current account for food.

say: I'd say **AI draft checks** are useful only after tests on nameless records.
I'd tell colleagues that **appointment dates** still need careful review.
think: I worry about **mortgage and school costs** with three weeks saved.
I know a lost **care night shift** could hurt us before AI does.
do: Keep checking **appointment imports** and asking a senior developer about risky fixes.
Use the **helper on test records** only, following a proven method.
Save **15 each payday** for school costs only while both sets of shifts hold.
feel: **Anxious** about ordinary household income, even under mild AI.
S0.quote: A missed night shift is more frightening this month than a forecast about code.
fieldNote: **Three weeks saved**, mortgage costs and care-shift variation already make the mild scenario anxious.

steps.text: Check appointment imports each morning and ask senior developer about risky fixes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firm should show which booking, coding and checking work AI will take before it talks about efficiency. My data-import checks are routine enough to be first on a list, and the care desk could change too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company keeps one experienced developer to check AI output, my junior seat could go. My partner's night shifts might hold, but one wage cannot cover the mortgage and childcare, and another software job is not just around the corner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the senior developer for a month of guided practice checking AI-made imports on old nameless data, and record which appointment dates it gets wrong. If my hours are cut in the first year, my partner and I would check whether any extra night shifts actually exist before changing childcare; we'd cancel our paid weekend activities before a mortgage payment slipped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can learn to check AI-made appointments, but I don't know whether anyone will pay a junior to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would have to happen before your partner took more shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not put our younger child in a longer after-school session just because a manager says more shifts may appear. We'd book longer after-school care only if a confirmed rota pays more than the childcare fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the senior developer to teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The senior developer showed me one safe test last spring, so I would ask for more of that. I would bring the wrong-date example rather than ask for a general promise that my job is safe.

I'd say **routine imports** and perhaps care-desk work could change quickly.
think: I fear **my junior seat** could disappear while a senior checks AI output.
I know one remaining wage cannot cover **mortgage and childcare**.
do: Practice **AI-made import checks** for a month on old nameless data if a senior guides me.

Cancel **paid weekend activities** before missing a mortgage payment.
feel: **Alarmed** about both my post and the household's ability to pay.

fieldNote: **Routine import checking** is exposed early, and his partner's care hours may not cover the mortgage alone.

steps.text: Practice checking AI imports on old nameless records for a month if senior guides

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 reaches appointment code and checks straight away; hands-on robots around 2031 would come later. I want to know who answers a patient when an automated booking is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a junior import job could be cut fast. We have roughly three weeks saved, a mortgage and two children, and my partner's care wage cannot safely carry all of that; the few local developer openings could disappear with the same change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check our mortgage statement now and ask the lender about hardship options before any missed payment. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply for paid clinic reception work only if there is a vacancy and the wage plus my partner's confirmed shifts covers mortgage and childcare; if none meets that test, I'd ask my former warehouse supervisor and apply only if paid shifts actually exist and household wages cover mortgage and childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. The tools may be clever, but I cannot put an AI answer in the mortgage account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a warehouse shift actually available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warehouse supervisor knows me from before college, but we have not discussed a return. I would ask about actual hours and pay, then compare the cost of childcare before accepting anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children that school and dinner are the priorities. I would not promise that the house is safe forever, but I would not frighten them with a move we have not decided.

say: I'd say **2028 thinking AI** reaches appointment code before 2031 robots.
I'd ask who handles **wrong automated bookings** for patients.
think: I expect **my junior import role** could end quickly.
I cannot cover **mortgage and childcare** for long on three weeks saved.
do: Ask the **mortgage lender** now about hardship options before a missed payment.
After a cut, apply for **clinic reception** only if a paid vacancy and household wages cover mortgage and childcare.
Seek **paid warehouse vacancies** if no clinic job qualifies and household wages cover mortgage and childcare.
feel: **Alarmed** by a possible quick wage loss and a short buffer.
S2.quote: I cannot put an AI answer in the mortgage account.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AI** hits appointment coding directly; later robots do not delay his own risk.
He checks **wages and childcare**, treating the old warehouse contact as an enquiry rather than a promised job.

steps.text: Ask mortgage lender now about hardship terms before missing payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 gives us a chance to see how many booking checks still need people. Robots come around 2034, but thinking AI reaches my desk work in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could get better at checking faulty imports if I learn steadily, but the company could still choose a smaller team. Five years may let us build a buffer if both wages hold; it does not erase the mortgage we pay next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a weekly half-hour with the senior developer to check one AI-made import on test data, if the team can spare that time. We'd put 15 per payday into the school pot while both rosters hold, and in the first year after 2031 I'd apply for paid clinic scheduling posts only if they exist and the household pay covers mortgage and childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I can work through one example a week. I would rather know the error rate than guess whether I am employable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go into your weekly practice record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weekly example should include a date-format error and what a patient would actually see. I'd write down the test and have the senior check my result before I put it in my job record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the care rota shrinks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would check the night rota every month. If care hours fell, we'd stop the school-pot transfer rather than borrow to keep it looking tidy.

I'd ask for **measured error rates** while we still have years to learn.
think: I could improve at **checking imports**, but a smaller team may still cut me.
I need **both rosters** to hold before a larger buffer becomes real.
do: Practice **weekly AI import checks** if a senior can spare half an hour.
Save **15 each payday** only while both work rosters hold.
After 2031, apply for **paid clinic scheduling** only if posts exist and household pay covers mortgage and childcare.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to build skill one test at a time.

fieldNote: **Five years** enable supervised practice, but his junior standing and mortgage keep his own income at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 is a chance to learn the whole appointment route, not just the import screen. Thinking AI still reaches code before the 2039 robots, so our team should not wait for the robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I could have built a stable scheduling role, if paid clinics still need people to explain errors. I could also be in the same lower-paid junior seat until it disappears. The mortgage and school expenses still arrive now. Three weeks of savings is not peace of mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the weekly test practice if the senior has time and add patient-facing scheduling rules to my notebook. If both incomes hold, we'd save 15 each payday and put any extra overtime pay toward the mortgage; in the first year after 2036 I'd compare actual paid scheduling and software offers, moving only if the new wage with my partner's confirmed hours covers mortgage and childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today's bills, though the far date gives me a chance to learn at a pace I can manage. I won't plan a house move from a headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a patient need from your notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a patient to be able to ask why an appointment moved and get a plain answer. My notebook would show the wrong-date test and the fix, not anyone's medical details.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the children's study plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children may be grown by then, but we still need to get through next term's school costs. I would talk with them about future studies when we know fees and their interests, not around a guess about AI.

I'd ask for **plain appointment explanations** for patients.
think: I might build **paid scheduling work** if clinics still need people.

S4.quote: Three weeks of savings is not peace of mind.
fieldNote: **Ten years** do not remove current household pressure from low pay, a mortgage and a thin buffer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the routine import work could go before I have enough saved to search. A clear notice period, mortgage breathing room and a real paid opening with workable childcare would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how a wrong date feels to the person waiting at a clinic. A patient can lose a day of work because our file put an appointment on Tuesday instead of Thursday.

headlineQuote: A patient can lose a day of work because our file put an appointment on Tuesday instead of Thursday.
portrait: Rafael, **43**, moved from warehouse work through a two-year diploma into junior software development for clinic appointments.
His **lower pay**, three-week cushion and variable care night shifts strain a mortgage and two school-age children's costs.
He sometimes uses **AI on test data**, seeking senior review after a suggested fix nearly moved every afternoon slot.
Steady disruption **alarms** him because routine imports could move to software while his family's childcare costs remain.
With more time, he practices **weekly checks**, saves only when both rosters hold and requires real paid jobs covering household costs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his routine import work before his short cushion supports a search.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear notice**, mortgage breathing room and a paid vacancy with workable childcare would help.
